outcomes.text: Know that two religions are studied from the seven offered, and that Christianity with Catholic Christianity is not allowed.
Recognise that Britain's main tradition is Christian but its religions are diverse.
Study Buddhist beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (Theravada, Mahayana, Zen, Pure Land).
Explain the concept of Dhamma and dependent arising (paticcasamupada).
Describe the Three Marks of Existence: anicca, anatta and dukkha.
Compare the human personality in Theravada (Five Aggregates) and Mahayana (sunyata, Buddha-nature).
Compare Arhat and Bodhisattva ideals, and ideas of Buddhahood and the Pure Land.

subtopics.title: The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths

outcomes.text: Outline the Buddha's life: birth in luxury, the Four Sights, ascetic life and Enlightenment, and why it matters.
Explain the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its causes (the Three Poisons), the end of craving and nibbana.
Describe the Eightfold Path as the Threefold Way of ethics, meditation and wisdom.
Describe Buddhist places of worship and their key features such as Buddha rupas, artefacts and offerings.
Explain the role of puja, chanting, mantras and malas at home and in the temple.
Compare meditation types: samatha, vipassana and zazen, and the visualisation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Describe death and mourning ceremonies in Theravada communities, Japan and Tibet.
Explain the origins and importance of Wesak and Parinirvana Day, and of retreats, for British Buddhists.
Explain kamma and rebirth, compassion (karuna) and loving kindness (metta) as ethical teaching.
Describe the five moral precepts.
Describe the six perfections in Mahayana and how a person develops them.
Study Christian beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant).

subtopics.title: Nature of God, creation and afterlife

outcomes.text: Explain God as omnipotent, loving and just, the problem of evil, and God as Trinity.
Compare Christian beliefs about creation, including Word and Spirit.
Compare beliefs about the afterlife: resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell.
Explain beliefs about the incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension.
Explain sin, original sin, the means of salvation (law, grace, Spirit) and atonement.
Compare liturgical, non-liturgical, informal and private worship, and the use of the Bible.
Explain the importance of prayer, including the Lord's Prayer, set prayers and informal prayer.
Explain what a sacrament is, and the significance of baptism, including infant and believers' baptism.
Explain Holy Communion/Eucharist and different views of its meaning.
Compare pilgrimage to Lourdes and Iona.
Explain the importance of Christmas and Easter for British Christians.

subtopics.title: The Church in the community and world

outcomes.text: Describe the Church's local role, such as food banks and street pastors.
Explain mission, evangelism and Church growth.
Explain the worldwide Church's work: reconciliation, responses to persecution, and one development charity (CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund).
Study Catholic beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (Orthodox and Protestant views).
Explain God as Trinity, the Nicene Creed and the Council of Nicaea.
Explain Genesis 1 and 2 on creation, human dignity and humanity's relation to creation.
Explain the incarnation: Jesus as fully God and fully human.
Explain redemption through Jesus's life, death, resurrection and ascension, and grace.
Describe beliefs about life after death including purgatory.
Explain the meaning of sacrament and the sacramental nature of reality.
Describe the names, meanings and effects of the seven sacraments, and views on the eucharist as source and summit.
Explain prayer as raising the mind and heart to God, formal and informal prayer, and the Lord's Prayer.
Explain the Rosary and Stations of the Cross.
Explain pilgrimage with one Catholic example, and the funeral rite.
Explain the duty to love our neighbour through Catholic social teaching, including Gaudium et Spes 26, and justice, peace and reconciliation.
Describe Catholic agencies CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio.
Explain mission and evangelism for Catholics today.
Explain the aims of the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul and of Corrymeela or Pax Christi.
Study Hindu beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (Shaivism, Vaishnavism).
Explain different understandings of brahman: nirguna, saguna and spiritual worlds.
Explain the three features of the divine: everywhere, within the heart and beyond.
Describe how the divine presents: Tri-murti, deities and avatara such as Krishna and Rama.
Explain prakriti, the three gunas, maya, cosmology and the four ages.
Explain atman, samsara, karma and moksha.
Discuss free will, responses to suffering, knowledge and ignorance, and personal virtues such as ahimsa.
Explain the four aims of life, and dharma, sanatana dharma and varnashrama dharma.
Describe places of worship: home, temple, outdoor shrines and the heart.
Explain forms of worship such as havan, puja, arati, darshan, bhajan and japa, with Shaivite and Vaishnavite differences.
Explain the focuses of worship, including deities, gurus, sacred places and the murti.
Explain the origins and meaning of Diwali and Holi.
Compare the four yoga paths: karma, jnana, astanga and bhakti.
Explain pilgrimage, Varanasi and Kumbh Mela.
Describe Hindu environmental projects, cow protection and charities for well-being, inclusion and women's rights.
Study Muslim beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (Sunni and Shi'a).
Compare the six articles of faith in Sunni Islam with the five roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam.
Explain Tawhid and Surah 112.
Explain God's nature: omnipotence, mercy, justice and Adalat, immanence and transcendence.
Explain the nature and role of angels such as Jibril and Mika'il.
Explain predestination, human freedom and the Day of Judgement.
Explain Akhirah: accountability, resurrection, heaven and hell.
Explain Risalah and the roles of Adam, Ibrahim and Muhammad.
Explain the Qur'an's revelation and authority, and other holy books.
Explain the role of the imamate in Shi'a Islam.
Compare the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam with the Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi'a Islam.
Explain the Shahadah and its place in practice.
Explain how and why Muslims pray, including wudu, rak'ahs, Jummah and Sunni-Shi'a differences.
Explain sawm in Ramadan: origins, duties, benefits, exceptions and the Night of Power.
Explain zakah and Khums.
Describe how hajj is performed and the significance of its sites.
Explain greater and lesser jihad and conditions for lesser jihad.
Explain the origins and meaning of Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr and Ashura for British Muslims.
Study Jewish beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (Orthodox, Reform, Liberal).
Explain God as one, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge, and the Shekhinah.
Explain beliefs about life after death, judgement and resurrection.
Explain different views of the Messiah.
Explain the Covenant with Abraham and the promised land (Genesis 12:1-3).
Explain the Covenant at Sinai, Moses and the Ten Commandments.
Explain key moral principles: justice, healing the world, charity and kindness.
Explain the sanctity of life and Pikuach Nefesh.
Explain free will and the 613 mitzvot, including the two types of mitzvot.
Describe the synagogue's importance and features: bimah, aron hakodesh and ner tamid, and Orthodox-Reform differences.
Explain public worship, the Amidah, and synagogue services.
Explain Shabbat at home and synagogue, and private and home worship.
Explain the Tenakh and Talmud and their use in daily life.
Describe Jewish rituals: Brit Milah, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, marriage and mourning.
Explain kosher and trefah and separation of milk and meat.
Explain the origins and meaning of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Pesach.
Study Sikh beliefs, teachings and practices and their basis in its sources of authority, with scripture where fitting.
Explain how these shape individuals, communities and societies, and compare common and divergent views (sahajdhari and amritdhari).
Explain the Mool Mantra and its significance (GGS 1a).
Explain God as Creator, shown in and separate from the universe.
Explain human life as a chance to unite with God, and Sikh virtues.
Explain karma, rebirth and mukti, including positive and negative aspects.
Explain the five khands and barriers to mukti.
Contrast gurmukh and manmukh, and the removal of haumai.
Explain the oneness of humanity and equality of all, including women, as shown in the Gurus' lives, the GGS and Sikhism today.
Explain sewa as physical, mental and material service.
Explain the role of the sangat.
Describe the gurdwara's features, palki and takht, and its role in the community.
Explain prayer at home (GGS 305:4) and the akhand path.
Explain langar as sewa and the practice of nam japna.
Explain Vaisakhi, Divali and gurpurbs, including differences between India and Britain.
Explain the importance of visiting historical gurdwaras such as the Golden Temple.
Describe birth and naming ceremonies.
Explain Amrit Sanskar, the Khalsa and five Ks, and the names Singh and Kaur.
Know that four themes are studied: four religious, philosophical and ethical studies themes, or two plus the two textual studies themes.
Consider religious and non-religious views, such as atheism and humanism, and the arguments and their influence on the modern world.
Apply religious teachings with references to scripture and sacred texts.
Know that British traditions are mainly Christian yet diverse.
Explain contrasting beliefs on contraception, sex before marriage and same-sex relationships, using Christianity and another tradition.
Discuss human sexuality, and sexual relationships before and outside marriage.
Discuss contraception and family planning.
Explain the nature and purpose of marriage, same-sex marriage and cohabitation.
Discuss divorce, its reasons, remarriage and ethical arguments about it.
Describe the nature of families: roles of parents and children, extended and nuclear families.
Explain the purposes of families: procreation, protecting children and educating in faith.
Discuss same-sex parents and polygamy.
Discuss the roles of men and women, gender equality, and gender prejudice and discrimination.

subtopics.title: Origins and value of the universe

outcomes.text: Explain contrasting beliefs on abortion, euthanasia and animal experimentation, using Christianity and another tradition.
Explain religious teachings on the universe's origins and how they relate to the Big Bang theory.
Explain stewardship, dominion, responsibility and awe, and the value of the world.
Discuss use and abuse of the environment, natural resources and pollution.
Discuss use and abuse of animals, experimentation and food.

subtopics.title: Origins and value of human life

outcomes.text: Explain religious teachings on human life's origins and how they relate to evolution.
Explain the sanctity of life and quality of life.
Discuss abortion, including when the mother's life is at risk, and the ethical arguments.
Discuss euthanasia.
Explain how beliefs about death and afterlife affect views on the value of life.

topics.title: 3.2.1.3 Theme C: The existence of God and revelation

subtopics.title: Arguments about the existence of God

outcomes.text: Explain contrasting beliefs on visions, miracles and nature as general revelation, using Christianity and non-religious beliefs.
Evaluate the Design argument.
Evaluate the First Cause argument.
Evaluate the argument from miracles, with one example.
Explain evil and suffering as an argument against God.
Explain science-based arguments against the existence of God.
Explain special revelation, including visions, with one example.
Explain enlightenment as a source of knowledge about the divine.
Explain general revelation through nature and scripture.
Compare ideas of the divine: omnipotent and omniscient, personal and impersonal, immanent and transcendent.
Evaluate the value of revelation and enlightenment, including problems and alternative explanations.

topics.title: 3.2.1.4 Theme D: Religion, peace and conflict

outcomes.text: Explain contrasting beliefs on violence, weapons of mass destruction and pacifism, using Christianity and another tradition.
Explain the meaning of peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation.
Discuss violence, including violent protest, and terrorism.
Explain reasons for war: greed, self-defence and retaliation.
Explain just war theory and its criteria.
Explain holy war and pacifism.
Discuss religion and belief as a cause of war and violence today.
Discuss nuclear weapons, deterrence and weapons of mass destruction.
Describe religious peace-making by individuals.
Describe religious responses to victims of war, including one organisation's work.

topics.title: 3.2.1.5 Theme E: Religion, crime and punishment

outcomes.text: Explain contrasting beliefs on corporal punishment, the death penalty and forgiveness, using Christianity and another tradition.
Discuss good and evil intentions and actions, and whether causing suffering can be good.
Explain reasons for crime: poverty, mental health, addiction, greed, hate and unjust laws.
Compare views on types of crime: hate crime, theft and murder.
Explain the aims of punishment: retribution, deterrence and reformation.
Discuss treatment of criminals: prison, corporal punishment and community service.
Explain religious teachings on forgiveness.
Discuss the death penalty, including arguments on utility and sanctity of life.

topics.title: 3.2.1.6 Theme F: Religion, human rights and social justice

outcomes.text: Explain contrasting beliefs on the status of women in religion, the uses of wealth and freedom of religious expression.
Discuss prejudice and discrimination in religion, including women and same-sex relationships.
Discuss equality and freedom of religion and belief.
Explain human rights and their responsibilities, and social justice.
Discuss racial prejudice and discrimination, including positive discrimination.
Discuss the right attitude to wealth and its uses.
Explain the responsibilities of wealth, including tackling poverty.
Discuss exploitation: fair pay, excessive interest and people-trafficking.
Discuss the responsibility of the poor to help themselves.
Discuss charity and giving money to those in poverty.
Know that textual studies requires Christianity or Catholic Christianity in Component 1, and both Themes G and H.
Explain the influence and authority of St Mark's Gospel, varied interpretations and its relevance today.

topics.title: 3.2.2.1 Theme G: St Mark's gospel: the life of Jesus

outcomes.text: Study John's preparation and Jesus's baptism and temptation (Mark 1:1-13).
Study the paralysed man and Jairus' daughter (Mark 2:1-12; 5:21-43).
Study the rejection at Nazareth and feeding of the five thousand (Mark 6:1-6, 30-44).
Study Caesarea Philippi and the transfiguration (Mark 8:27-33; 9:2-9).
Study the passion prediction and the request of James and John (Mark 10:32-45).
Study Bartimaeus and the entry into Jerusalem (Mark 10:46-52; 11:1-11).
Study the Last Supper and Gethsemane (Mark 14:12-52).
Study the trials before the Jewish authorities and Pilate (Mark 14:53-65; 15:1-15).
Study the crucifixion, burial and empty tomb (Mark 15:21-47; 16:1-8).
Explain the titles Son of Man, Son of God, Christ and Son of David for 1st century Jews, Jesus and Christians today.
Explain Mark's portrayal of Jesus as teacher and miracle worker, and views on the miracle stories' historicity.
Compare beliefs about the Last Supper, Jesus's death and resurrection, and the empty tomb.
Evaluate the authority of Mark on Jesus's life against secular authority.

topics.title: 3.2.2.2 Theme H: St Mark's Gospel as a source of religious, moral and spiritual truths

outcomes.text: Study the parables of the sower, growing seed and mustard seed (Mark 4).
Study Jesus and the children, the rich man and the greatest commandment (Mark 10:13-27; 12:28-34).

subtopics.title: Jesus and those disregarded by society

outcomes.text: Study the man with leprosy, the call of Levi and the Greek woman's daughter (Mark 1:40-45; 2:13-17; 7:24-30).
Study the epileptic boy, the widow at the treasury and the anointing at Bethany (Mark 9:14-29; 12:41-44; 14:1-9).
Study the call of the first disciples, the woman with a haemorrhage and the mission of the Twelve (Mark 1:16-20; 5:24-34; 6:7-13).
Study the cost of discipleship, Peter's denials and the commission and ascension (Mark 8:34-38; 10:28-31; 14:27-31, 66-72; 16:14-20).
Explain the importance of key events in Jesus's life for Jesus, his contemporaries and people today.
Compare ways of understanding the Kingdom of God: present or future, inner state or community.
Explain attitudes to the disregarded in the 1st century and by Jesus, and their importance for Christians.
Compare views on discipleship and on the nature of faith.
Evaluate the authority of Jesus's teaching in Mark against secular authority.
